title: 3-Read Friday #6: Participation Ratios, Go-To Guides, and Classroom Success
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Issue six is a run of pedagogy-focused reading. Barton opens with InnerDrive's collaboration with Doug Lemov on "thinking and participation ratios," praising the accompanying graphic and singling out the "Shallow Land" and "Sparse Participation" labels as ones he recognizes in his own teaching. He then covers Craig Latimir's "Go-to Guides," department planning documents covering overview, topic familiarisation, hinterland, and possible models, which Barton calls the most comprehensive resource of its kind he's seen. He closes with Jo Castelino's "Thoughts on success in the classroom," which opens by dismantling conventional success criteria in favour of identifying discrete "moments of success" students can experience. All three items concern instructional design and classroom pedagogy, making this the most unambiguously Learning & Curriculum issue of the batch.
points: Barton singles out the "Shallow Land" and "Sparse Participation" labels from the Lemov/InnerDrive graphic as descriptions he personally recognizes in his own lessons.
He calls Latimir's Go-to Guides the most comprehensive planning resource he has seen a Head of Maths use, ahead of PowerPoints or spreadsheet-based schemes of work.
He credits Castelino with reframing success away from static success criteria and toward identifying the specific moments in a lesson where a student can feel successful.
quotes: First, there is a lovely graphic to help teachers reflect on the current ratio in their lessons. Then there are Shallow Land and Sparse Participation, descriptions which I certainly recognise in my own teaching.
I have never seen anything as comprehensive, nor as useful, as these Go-to Guides by Craig Latimir.
With sections such as Overview, Topic Familiarisation, Hinterland and Possible Models, teachers of all levels of experience have everything they need to support their planning.
This one challenges us to consider what it means for students to be successful in our lessons, and what steps we can take to help more students feel more successful.
The blog starts with a dismantling of success criteria, suggesting instead we look for the different moments of success students could experience.
